title: Logarithmic scales and linearizing data
summary: A [[logarithmic-scale|logarithmic scale]] spaces values by multiplying factors, so data from $0.01$ to $1\,000\,000$ fit on one graph. Taking logs also straightens curved data: a straight line on a [[semi-log-graph|semi-log graph]] means an exponential model, and on a [[log-log-graph|log-log graph]] a power model. The line's [[gradient|gradient]] and intercept give you the model's [[parameter|parameters]].

goals.text: Choose a logarithmic scale for data with a very wide range or when growth rates matter, and read values off a log axis.
Linearize exponential data by plotting $\ln y$ against $x$, then find $k$ and $a$ in $y = ka^{x}$ from the best-fit line.
Linearize power data by plotting $\ln y$ against $\ln x$, then find $k$ and $n$ in $y = kx^{n}$.
Interpret the gradient and intercept of semi-log and log-log graphs in context.
Decide between an exponential and a power model by comparing $r$ for the two linearized data sets, and justify the choice.

before.hint: Use the product law first, then the power law on $x^{3}$ only.
before.explain: $\ln\left(4x^{3}\right) = \ln 4 + \ln x^{3} = \ln 4 + 3\ln x$. The power $3$ belongs to $x$ only, so $3\ln(4x)$ is wrong. Revise it in {{lesson:1.9}}.

before.prompt: Find $\log_{10}\left(3.2 \times 10^{5}\right)$. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
before.explain: $\log_{10} 3.2 = 0.505\ldots$, so the log is $5.505\ldots \approx 5.51$. The power of ten gives the whole number part. Revise it in {{lesson:1.5}}.

before.prompt: A [[regression-line|regression line]] has $r = -0.995$. What does this tell you about the data?
before.hint: The sign gives the direction. The size gives how close the points are to a line.
before.explain: $r$ near $-1$ means the points lie close to a falling line. Revise it in {{lesson:4.4}}.

blocks.text: Animal masses run from grams to over $100$ tonnes. On an ordinary axis, every small animal piles up at $0$.
A [[logarithmic-scale|logarithmic scale]] fixes this. Each gridline is $10$ times the one before, so equal distances stand for equal multiplying factors, not equal differences.

blocks.statement: A scale on which a value $v > 0$ is placed at distance proportional to $\log_{10} v$. Moving along by the length of one power of ten multiplies the value by $10$.
blocks.plain: Each step along the axis multiplies by the same factor.

blocks.alt: A horizontal log axis with equally spaced gridlines labelled 1, 10, 100, 1000 and 10 000, and an arc marked times 10 between each pair. Smaller ticks for 2 to 9 crowd towards the right of each gap. A dot halfway between 10 and 100 is labelled 31.6 is halfway, and a dashed pointer shows that 55 sits much closer to 100.
blocks.caption: Equal gaps are equal factors. The midpoint of the $10$ to $100$ gap is $10^{1.5} \approx 31.6$.

blocks.text: To read a log axis, use exponents: a point a fraction $p$ of the way from $10^{a}$ to $10^{a+1}$ shows $10^{a + p}$.

blocks.question: A chart shows the annual rainfall at weather stations on a $\log_{10}$ axis, in mm. One station's point sits a quarter of the way from the $100$ gridline to the $1000$ gridline. Find its rainfall, to 3 s.f.
steps: The $100$ gridline is at exponent $2$ and the $1000$ gridline at exponent $3$.
A quarter of the way along adds $0.25$ to the exponent: $2 + 0.25 = 2.25$.
The value is $10^{2.25} = 177.82\ldots$, so about $178$ mm.
Reading the axis as linear would wrongly give $325$ mm.

blocks.question: A pygmy shrew has mass $0.004$ kg and a blue whale $140\,000$ kg. On a $\log_{10}$ axis drawn with $1.5$ cm for each power of ten, how far apart are the two animals? Give your answer to 3 s.f.
steps: Positions are $\log_{10}$ of the masses, so the gap is $\log_{10} 140\,000 - \log_{10} 0.004$.
By the quotient law this is $\log_{10}\left(\frac{140\,000}{0.004}\right) = \log_{10}\left(3.5 \times 10^{7}\right) = 7.544\ldots$
Each power of ten takes $1.5$ cm: $7.544\ldots \times 1.5 = 11.316\ldots$, so about $11.3$ cm.
Interpret: both animals fit on one page.

blocks.text: Log scales also show growth rates. With a log vertical axis and time across, constant percentage growth is a straight line.
A steeper line means faster percentage growth, whatever the size of the numbers.

blocks.alt: Graph of cases on a log scale from 10 to 100 000 against days from 0 to 40. Line A starts at 2000 and rises gently to 8000. Line B starts at 20 and rises steeply to 5000. Both are straight. B stays below A but is much steeper.
blocks.caption: Country A has more cases, but country B's cases grow faster in percentage terms.

blocks.text: Subtracting two readings on a log axis as if the gap were the difference in values. A gap on a log axis is a ratio: convert each reading to a value first.

blocks.prompt: On a $\log_{10}$ axis, a point sits $60\%$ of the way from the $100$ gridline to the $1000$ gridline. What value does it show? Give your answer to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: Add $0.6$ to the exponent of the lower gridline.
blocks.explain: The exponent is $2 + 0.6 = 2.6$, so the value is $10^{2.6} = 398.1\ldots \approx 398$. Reading it as linear gives $640$, which is wrong.

blocks.prompt: In the figure above, which country's cases are growing faster in percentage terms?
blocks.hint: On a log scale, the gradient shows the growth rate, not the height of the line.

options.text: both grow at the same rate

blocks.explain: B's line is steeper, so its cases multiply by a larger factor each day. A has more cases but grows more slowly.

blocks.text: [[linearizing-data|Linearizing data]] means taking logs so that curved data lie on a straight line. You used the log laws for this in {{lesson:1.9}}.
Suppose $y = ka^{x}$ with $k > 0$ and $a > 0$. Taking $\ln$ of both sides gives $\ln y = \ln k + x\ln a$. So $\ln y$ against $x$ is a straight line.

A graph of $\ln y$ (or $\log_{10} y$) against $x$ is a [[semi-log-graph|semi-log graph]]. If its points lie close to a straight line with gradient $m$ and intercept $c$, then $a = \mathrm{e}^{m}$ and $k = \mathrm{e}^{c}$.
With $\log_{10} y$, use $a = 10^{m}$ and $k = 10^{c}$ instead. The model can also be written $y = k\mathrm{e}^{mx}$.

blocks.statement: A graph with a logarithmic scale on one axis only, usually the vertical axis, or a plot of $\ln y$ against $x$.
blocks.plain: One axis is logged; exponential data look straight.

blocks.question: A new online account's followers $F$ were counted each week. The graph of $\log_{10} F$ against the week number $w$ is a straight line through $(0, 2.6)$ and $(10, 3.8)$. Write $F$ in the form $ka^{w}$, and interpret $a$.
steps: So $k = 10^{2.6} = 398.1\ldots$ and $a = 10^{0.12} = 1.318\ldots$, giving $F \approx 398 \times 1.32^{w}$.
Interpret: $k$ is the model's follower count at the start, about $398$. Each week $F$ is multiplied by $1.318\ldots$, a growth of about $32\%$ a week.

blocks.question: The concentration $C$ (mg per litre) of a medicine in a patient's blood is measured $t$ hours after a dose. $\begin{array}{c|cccccc} t & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline C & 8.1 & 5.9 & 4.4 & 3.2 & 2.4 & 1.7 \end{array}$ Find the regression line of $\ln C$ on $t$. Hence write $C$ in the form $k\mathrm{e}^{bt}$, with $k$ and $b$ to 3 s.f.
steps: Take $\ln$ of every $C$ value: $\ln 8.1 = 2.0919\ldots$, $\ln 5.9 = 1.7749\ldots$, and so on. Enter $t$ in one list and $\ln C$ in another.
Linear regression of $\ln C$ on $t$ gives $\ln C = -0.309230\ldots t + 2.40191\ldots$, with $r = -0.9997\ldots$, so the line fits very well.
Undo the logs: $C = \mathrm{e}^{2.40191\ldots} \times \mathrm{e}^{-0.309230\ldots t}$, so $k = 11.044\ldots$ and $b = -0.309230\ldots$
So $C \approx 11.0\mathrm{e}^{-0.309t}$. Interpret: each hour $C$ is multiplied by $\mathrm{e}^{-0.309\ldots} = 0.734\ldots$, so it falls by about $27\%$ an hour.

blocks.text: Write down that you used $\ln C$, not $C$. The regression of $C$ on $t$ is a different line and earns no marks here.

blocks.prompt: Data give a semi-log line, $\ln y$ on $x$, sloping downwards. Which model fits the data?
blocks.hint: A straight line on a semi-log graph means $y = ka^{x}$. What does a negative gradient say about $a$?
blocks.explain: The gradient is $\ln a$. A negative gradient means $\ln a < 0$, so $0 < a < 1$: exponential decay.

blocks.prompt: A town's population $P$, $t$ years after 2020, fits the line $\ln P = 0.042t + 9.1$. By what percentage does the model's population grow each year? Give your answer to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: Each year $\ln P$ rises by $0.042$, so $P$ is multiplied by $\mathrm{e}^{0.042}$.
blocks.explain: $\mathrm{e}^{0.042} = 1.04289\ldots$, so $P$ grows by about $4.29\%$ a year. The intercept doesn't affect the rate.

blocks.text: Now suppose $y = kx^{n}$, with $k > 0$ and $x > 0$. Taking $\ln$ of both sides gives $\ln y = \ln k + n\ln x$. So $\ln y$ against $\ln x$ is a straight line.

blocks.tex: y = kx^{n} \;\Rightarrow\; \ln y = n\ln x + \ln k

blocks.text: A graph that logs both axes is a [[log-log-graph|log-log graph]]. The gradient is the power $n$. The intercept is $\ln k$ (or $\log_{10} k$ if both axes use base $10$).

blocks.statement: A graph with logarithmic scales on both axes, or a plot of $\ln y$ against $\ln x$. Data from $y = kx^{n}$, with $k > 0$ and $x > 0$, lie on a straight line with gradient $n$.
blocks.plain: Both axes are logged; power data look straight.

blocks.text: $n = 1$ is [[direct-variation|direct variation]], $n = -1$ is [[inverse-variation|inverse variation]], and $n = 2$ means doubling $x$ multiplies $y$ by $4$.

blocks.alt: Log-log graph of metabolic rate B in watts against body mass M in kilograms, both axes marked 1, 10, 100 and 1000. A straight line rises from the point (1, 3.4) through the point (100, 108) to about 600 watts at 1000 kilograms.
blocks.caption: On log-log axes, a straight line means $B = kM^{n}$.

blocks.question: For mammals, a log-log graph of resting metabolic rate $B$ (watts) against body mass $M$ (kg) is a straight line through the points $(1, 3.4)$ and $(100, 108)$, as in the figure. Find $n$ in $B = kM^{n}$, then estimate $B$ for a $40$ kg mammal, to 3 s.f.
steps: The axes are logged, so find the gradient from the logs of the coordinates: $n = \frac{\log_{10} 108 - \log_{10} 3.4}{\log_{10} 100 - \log_{10} 1} = \frac{\log_{10} 31.76\ldots}{2} = 0.75097\ldots$
At $M = 1$, $B = k \times 1^{n} = k$, so $k = 3.4$.
Interpret: $n < 1$, so a $40$ kg mammal uses only about $16$ times the power of a $1$ kg one.

blocks.question: An engineer records the blade length $L$ (m) and the rated power $P$ (kW) of six wind turbines. $\begin{array}{c|cccccc} L & 10 & 20 & 30 & 45 & 60 & 80 \\ \hline P & 33 & 120 & 290 & 640 & 1190 & 2050 \end{array}$ Use power regression to write $P$ in the form $kL^{n}$, with $k$ and $n$ to 3 s.f. Interpret $n$.
steps: Enter $L$ and $P$ as lists. Power regression fits a straight line to $\ln P$ against $\ln L$.
The GDC gives $P = 0.315381\ldots \times L^{2.00387\ldots}$, with $r = 0.9997\ldots$ for the log-log line.
Interpret: $n \approx 2$, so power is close to proportional to $L^{2}$. Doubling the blade length multiplies the power by about $4$.

blocks.text: Reading the gradient straight off log-labelled axes as $\frac{108 - 3.4}{100 - 1}$. On log-log axes, take logs of both coordinates first.

blocks.prompt: A log-log line is $\ln y = 1.5\ln x + 0.4$, for $x > 0$. Which equation gives $y$?
blocks.explain: $\mathrm{e}^{1.5\ln x} = x^{1.5}$, so $y = \mathrm{e}^{0.4}x^{1.5} \approx 1.49x^{1.5}$. The intercept $0.4$ is $\ln k$, not $k$.

blocks.prompt: A log-log graph of a radio signal's strength $S$ against distance $d$ km from the mast is a straight line with gradient $-2$. When $d = 2$, $S = 45$. Find $S$ when $d = 5$.
blocks.hint: Gradient $-2$ means $S = kd^{-2}$. Use $d = 2$ to find $k$.
blocks.explain: $45 = k \times 2^{-2}$, so $k = 180$ and $S = \frac{180}{d^{2}}$. At $d = 5$, $S = \frac{180}{25} = 7.2$. This is inverse-square variation.

sections.heading: Exponential or power? Choosing the model

blocks.text: To decide which model fits, linearize the data both ways and see which graph is straighter.
1. Plot $\ln y$ against $x$ (semi-log). Straight means exponential.
2. Plot $\ln y$ against $\ln x$ (log-log). Straight means power.

3. Compare $r$, [[pearsons-product-moment-correlation-coefficient|Pearson's correlation coefficient]], for the two transformed data sets. Choose the one with $|r|$ closer to $1$, then use its [[regression-line|regression line]] for the [[parameter|parameters]].

blocks.statement: For data with $y > 0$ (and $x > 0$ for the log-log graph): if $\ln y$ against $x$ is closer to linear, choose $y = ka^{x}$. If $\ln y$ against $\ln x$ is closer to linear, choose $y = kx^{n}$.
blocks.why: Each model is straight under its own transformation, and $r$ measures how close to straight the points are.

blocks.text: Find $r$ for the transformed data, not the raw data. If neither graph is close to straight, neither model fits well.

blocks.question: A messaging app's users $U$ (thousands) are recorded $m$ months after launch. An analyst fits two lines. Graph A, $\ln U$ against $m$: gradient $0.186$, intercept $1.62$, $r = 0.997$. Graph B, $\ln U$ against $\ln m$: gradient $1.34$, intercept $1.05$, $r = 0.951$. Choose the better model, justify your choice, and write it as $U = k\mathrm{e}^{bm}$ or $U = km^{n}$.
steps: Graph A has $r = 0.997$, closer to $1$ than Graph B's $0.951$, so the semi-log graph is straighter.
So choose the exponential model: $\ln U = 0.186m + 1.62$.
Undo the logs: $U = \mathrm{e}^{1.62}\mathrm{e}^{0.186m}$, with $k = \mathrm{e}^{1.62} = 5.0530\ldots$ and $b = 0.186$.
Interpret: about $5050$ users at launch, and $\mathrm{e}^{0.186} = 1.204\ldots$, so users grow by about $20\%$ a month. This can't last, so long-term predictions are unreliable.

blocks.question: A club runner's best times $T$ (minutes) over distances $d$ (km) are shown. $\begin{array}{c|ccccc} d & 1.5 & 5 & 10 & 21.1 & 42.2 \\ \hline T & 4.6 & 17.0 & 35.2 & 77.5 & 165.0 \end{array}$ Decide whether an exponential or a power model fits better, giving a reason. Use it to estimate the runner's time for $30$ km, to 3 s.f.
steps: Semi-log: $r$ for $\ln T$ against $d$ is $0.90260\ldots$
Log-log: $r$ for $\ln T$ against $\ln d$ is $0.99997\ldots$, much closer to $1$. So choose the power model $T = kd^{n}$.
Power regression gives $T = 2.99879\ldots \times d^{1.06987\ldots}$.
At $d = 30$: $T = 2.99879\ldots \times 30^{1.06987\ldots} = 114.10\ldots$, so about $114$ minutes.
Interpret: $n$ is a little above $1$, so the runner's average pace slows slightly over longer races. $30$ km is inside the data, so the estimate is reasonable.

blocks.prompt: For a data set, $r = 0.981$ for $\ln y$ against $x$, and $r = 0.912$ for $\ln y$ against $\ln x$. Which model should you choose?
blocks.hint: Which transformation makes the data closer to a straight line?

options.text: a linear model in x and y

blocks.explain: The semi-log graph has $r$ closer to $1$, so the data are closer to $\ln y = mx + c$, which is an exponential model.

blocks.prompt: Hot soup cools in a room at $20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Its temperature is modelled by $T = ka^{t} + 20$. Before you fit $k$ and $a$ from the data by taking logs, what should you do?
blocks.hint: Taking logs works only on a pure product such as $ka^{t}$.

options.text: take ln of each temperature as it is

blocks.explain: $T - 20 = ka^{t}$, so $\ln(T - 20) = \ln k + t\ln a$ is linear in $t$. $\ln T$ is not, because the log of a sum can't be split.

blocks.text: On a $\log_{10}$ scale, equal steps are equal factors. A point a fraction $p$ of the way from $10^{a}$ to $10^{a+1}$ shows $10^{a+p}$.
With a log vertical axis and time across, a straight line means a constant percentage growth rate, and a steeper line means faster percentage growth.
If $y = ka^{x}$ with $k, a > 0$, then $\ln y = (\ln a)x + \ln k$: straight on a semi-log graph, with $a = \mathrm{e}^{\text{gradient}}$ and $k = \mathrm{e}^{\text{intercept}}$.
If $y = kx^{n}$ with $k > 0$ and $x > 0$, then $\ln y = n\ln x + \ln k$: straight on a log-log graph, with $n = $ gradient and $k = \mathrm{e}^{\text{intercept}}$.
With $\log_{10}$ in place of $\ln$, undo the logs with powers of $10$: $k = 10^{\text{intercept}}$, and $a = 10^{\text{gradient}}$ for an exponential model.
To choose between exponential and power models, find $r$ for $\ln y$ against $x$ and for $\ln y$ against $\ln x$. Choose the one with $|r|$ closer to $1$, and say so.
Keep the GDC's full gradient and intercept until you have undone the logs. Round only the final parameters and predictions.

mistakes: Running a linear regression of $y$ on $x$ when the question asks for $\ln y$ on $x$. Take $\ln$ of every $y$ value first; a line through the raw data is the wrong model.
Using the intercept $c$ as $k$. On a graph of $\ln y$ the intercept is $\ln k$, so $k = \mathrm{e}^{c}$; with $\log_{10} y$ it is $k = 10^{c}$.
Rounding the gradient or intercept before you undo the logs. Small changes in an exponent change $k$ and predictions a lot, so keep the GDC's full values.
Choosing a model with no reason. Quote $r$ (or $r^{2}$) for both linearized graphs and choose the one closer to $\pm 1$.
Reading a log axis as linear. Halfway between the $10$ and $100$ gridlines is $10^{1.5} \approx 31.6$, not $55$.
examTips: “Find the regression line in the form $\ln y = ax + b$”: write that you took $\ln$ of the $y$ values, then give the equation with $\ln y$ on the left and $a$ and $b$ to 3 s.f.
“Justify” a choice of model: state $r$ or $r^{2}$ for both linearized graphs and say which is closer to $1$ in size. A choice without a valid reason earns no marks.
“Interpret” a semi-log gradient as a growth or decay factor per unit of $x$, in context: “the concentration falls by about $27\%$ each hour”.
You won't be asked to draw or sketch log graphs, but you must read them. First check whether each axis shows the value or its log, and which base.
